To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the structure of the PA‐IL lectin in complex with galactic and calcium has been determined.
The crystal structures of Pseudomonasaeruginosa lectin 1 (PA‐IL), in complex with galatose, and of the native protein have been determined.

(a) PA‐IL adopts a β‐barrel fold, (b) calcium is essential for the binding of PA‐IL to galactose and (c) the calcium ion is co‐ordinated by all galactose hydroxy groups, except O‐1, and is located at the centre of a hydrogen bond network between the protein and the sugar
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and function of proteins and nucleic acids.
the structural biology and biochemistry of the P. aeruginosa lectins, PA‐I and PA‐II.
the molecular basis of calcium‐mediated recognition by bacterial lectins and with the structural basis of the interaction of bacterial lectins with their host receptors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work has shown that the structure of the complex between PA‐IL and calcium and galactoses is similar to the structures of other calcium galactose‐binding proteins.
the structure of PA‐IL in complex with Ca2+ and galactose is the first example of an invertebrate lectin with a calcium‐binding site.
PA‐IL has a calcium‐independent lectin activity and is a member of the legume lectin superfamily.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have determined the three‐dimensional structure of PA‐IL in complex with galactic acid and calcium and that the protein is a tetramer of dimers, with the calcium ion and the galactose ligand binding at the interface of the dimers.
the structure of the tetramer of PA‐IL in complex with calcium and galactosyl‐lactose has been determined at 1.

the crystal structure of PA‐IL in complex with gal and Ca2+ reveals that galactose binds in a deep pocket at the apex of each monomer, and the calcium ion is bound in a pocket formed by residues from two monomers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the PA‐IL structure is similar to that of the human C‐type lectin, and that the calcium and galactosyl moieties bind in a similar fashion to the protein.
calcium and galactoside binding are not necessarily mutually exclusive in lectins.
the calcium binding sites in PA‐IL and in the animal C‐type mannose binding lectins are very similar.
